speaker: Lisa Blatt
title: Arguing In Front of SCOTUS | Interview: Lisa Blatt
question: In Supreme Court oral argument, why do pre-planned jokes usually fail compared to spontaneous remarks?
guest: Absolutely not. There's no way, because anytime you attempt humor, it's a disaster. It just falls flat. It's such a bad idea, especially if you're not an experienced advocate. You just don't ever want to be funny, really. I think I was just staring at them, and it was more talking out loud. It was not an argument. I was just looking at them thinking, 'Wait a minute, I know you're not going to do this,' and that's just what came out. But maybe they will—hopefully they won't. And I did apologize and said, 'Sorry, maybe that was too much.' One of the things is, when you're not in the courtroom, you don't see what I'm seeing. I'm seeing their faces. I'm seeing a very comfortable court, a happy court, a court in a good mood, a playful court. They're not always like that. But this was a fun little precedent, and I didn't see it as impactful as the right to reproductive control over one's body, a la Dobbs and Roe.

points.core: Spontaneous remarks depend on reading the justices' live facial expressions in court.
points.note: Accept: gauging the bench's real-time mood, body language, or playfulness from the courtroom floor. Do not credit: generic advice to listen carefully to questions without noting live visual or mood cues.

points.core: Courtroom leeway for playful candor depends on the stakes of the precedent.
points.note: Accept: distinguishing lower-stakes technical precedents from momentous constitutional disputes when calibrating tone. Do not credit: blanket claims that informal tone works equally well in every Supreme Court case.

models.answer:
Pre-planned jokes tend to fail because oral argument is not a speech but a fast, justice-driven conversation, and a scripted line cuts against everything that makes humor work there.

First, humor in the courtroom depends on the moment. Laughter almost always arises from something that just happened: an odd hypothetical, a slip, an exchange between justices. A canned joke is disconnected from that flow, so it sounds forced and rehearsed, and the justices can tell.

Second, it violates the room's hierarchy. The justices make most of the jokes; advocates are there to answer questions. A lawyer who arrives with prepared material appears to be performing rather than helping the Court, which reads as presumptuous or as not taking the case seriously.

Third, it wastes scarce time and risks credibility. Every second spent on a set-up is taken from the argument, and if the joke lands flat, the awkward silence damages the advocate's rapport.

Spontaneous remarks, by contrast, show the advocate is listening and engaged. This is why veteran advocates and the Court's own guide for counsel warn against attempted humor, and suggest that any levity be brief, natural, and ideally self-deprecating.

models.answer:
Supreme Court oral argument is a rigorous, time-pressed conversation driven by the Justices, not a speech. Pre-planned jokes usually fail because they treat the lectern like a stage: they sound contrived, misread the room, and risk trivializing serious legal stakes, which is why the Court’s *Guide for Counsel* warns that "[a]ttempts at humor usually fall flat." Institutional hierarchy also works against scripted material. Because the Justices set the tone and initiate nearly all courtroom levity, an advocate who forces a rehearsed punchline can seem presumptuous or wasteful of scarce time, as infamously happened when counsel opened with a canned joke in *Roe v. Wade*.

Spontaneous remarks fare better because they arise naturally from the live exchange. When a lawyer meets a Justice’s pointed hypothetical or teasing aside with brief, understated wit or self-deprecation, it relieves tension while advancing the answer. Instead of pausing the argument for a performance, spontaneous humor respects the Court’s lead, stays tethered to the legal point, and signals composure and command of the case.

noweb.answer: In Supreme Court oral argument, pre-planned jokes usually fail because they clash with the proceeding’s formal decorum, power dynamics, and unpredictable rhythm. Unlike a speech, oral argument is an intense, rapid-fire conversation driven by the Justices’ questions. Inserting a rehearsed punchline disrupts that analytical flow, sounds forced, and risks making the advocate appear glib about high-stakes legal issues—which is why the Court’s official guide for counsel explicitly warns that attempts at humor usually fall flat. Courtroom levity also follows an unspoken hierarchy in which the Justices, not the advocates, set the tone. Spontaneous remarks succeed by contrast because they emerge organically from the immediate exchange, typically as quick, self-deprecating responses to a difficult hypothetical, a slip of the tongue, or a Justice’s own quip. Rather than halting the inquiry for a scripted performance, genuine wit briefly releases tension while respecting the bench’s authority and keeping the focus squarely on the argument.

models.answer:
Prepared jokes usually fail because oral argument is a conversation the Justices control, not a speech the lawyer delivers. Advocates have very little time, often 30 minutes split between sides, and the bench interrupts constantly. A rehearsed quip has to be forced into an exchange that has moved somewhere else, so it sounds contrived and uses up time the Court wanted spent on its questions. Scalia and Bryan Garner's advocacy guide *Making Your Case* warns lawyers against trying to be funny for this reason. The stakes are serious for the client, and a joke that falls flat or seems disrespectful can hurt the lawyer's credibility.

The power dynamic matters too. Jay Wexler's studies of "[laughter]" in transcripts found that the Justices produce most of the laughs, and advocates mostly react to them. A spontaneous remark works because it grows out of the exchange. It might be a light reply to a Justice's own joke, a bit of self-deprecation after a stumble, or a quick answer to a hypothetical. That kind of humor shows the lawyer is listening and at ease, and it can ease tension without pulling attention away from the legal argument.

In Supreme Court oral argument, pre-planned jokes usually fail because the courtroom is an unpredictable, high-stakes dialogue controlled by the justices rather than a scripted speech. Rapid-fire interruptions and shifting lines of questioning make it almost impossible to land a rehearsed line naturally; forcing one in feels contrived, breaks analytical momentum, and wastes precious argument time. Moreover, the bench sets the tone in such a formal setting, so scripted humor from an advocate risks seeming flippant, self-indulgent, or tone-deaf to the seriousness of the case—especially when a justice is pressing a difficult point.

Spontaneous remarks succeed for the opposite reason: they grow directly out of the live exchange. When an advocate reacts lightly to an unexpected hypothetical, a slip of the tongue, or a justice's own playful framing, the humor feels earned and authentic. Because it follows the bench's cues and stays tethered to the legal issue at hand, spontaneous wit releases tension and signals poise and mastery without ever seeming to compete with the Court.

noweb.answer:
In Supreme Court oral argument, pre-planned jokes usually fail because the proceeding is an unpredictable, high-stakes dialogue rather than a scripted speech. Justices interrupt frequently and steer the conversation in unexpected directions, so a rehearsed line rarely fits the moment naturally. When an advocate forces a prepared punchline into a serious exchange, it sounds contrived, breaks the conversational rhythm, and can suggest that the lawyer is performing rather than listening closely to the bench. Worse, scripted humor carries a high risk of seeming flippant about weighty legal issues or misreading the mood of the courtroom.

Spontaneous remarks succeed for the opposite reasons. A brief, organic witticism—such as a candid concession, a dry reaction to an extreme hypothetical, or a graceful recovery from a stumble—grows directly out of the justices' own questions. Because it is grounded in the exact moment, unscripted humor demonstrates composure, attentiveness, and intellectual agility. Rather than distracting from the merits, it briefly relieves tension while reinforcing the advocate's credibility.
